modalities.name: Bare Sensation Listening
modalities.tagline: Your felt sense in plain body words, right now, on your own.
modalities.whatItIs: Bare Sensation Listening is a new, untested concept that takes Focusing further away from guided imagery work. You attend to the vague bodily sense of your situation right now, but describe it only in plain sensation words such as tight, warm or heavy, with no pictures, stories or memories.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying with what the body is doing in the present, without turning it into images or history, may let a situation be felt freshly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit or lie down for 10 to 15 minutes and ask how a current situation feels in your body right now. Each time a word comes, check that it names a sensation (pressure, flutter, ache) rather than a picture or a memory, and let the sensation be as it is without asking it to change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a simple self-led practice and find imagery or digging into the past tiring.
modalities.cautions: Even plain body attention can bring up strong feelings, so open your eyes or stop if it becomes too much. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a qualified therapist, and this untested idea is not a substitute for treatment.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Bare Sensation Listening. You check how a situation feels in your body right now and describe it only in plain words like tight or warm. No images, no backstory. A simple, solo way to get clearer on what you feel.

modalities.name: Undivided Body Sense
modalities.tagline: Feel all of yourself as one whole, then settle.
modalities.whatItIs: Undivided Body Sense is a speculative practice that pushes Focusing away from parts-based therapy. Instead of sorting your inner life into parts or voices, you sense the body as one whole and ask how all of you is right now, which makes it quieter and more settling than ordinary Focusing.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling yourself as a single whole, rather than a crowd of competing parts, may offer a calm place to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 15 minutes, let your breath be, and ask "how is all of this, as one?" instead of picking out a single feeling. When an inner voice or part shows up, let it fold back into the whole sense of the body, and end by noticing the overall sense once more, whatever it is.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel pulled in many directions and want a gentle, self-led way to feel whole and wind down.
modalities.cautions: If one strong feeling or memory keeps coming forward, it may need more care than this offers, so pause and consider talking it through with a therapist. It is an untested concept and not a replacement for treatment of anxiety or depression.
modalities.tweet: An idea for busy minds: Undivided Body Sense. Lie down and ask how all of you feels, as one whole, instead of sorting yourself into parts and voices. A quiet, self-led way to settle. Untested, just something to try.

modalities.name: Let the Body Choose
modalities.tagline: No topic, no steps, no goal: the body sets the agenda.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Body Choose is a new concept that strips Focusing of its steps and goals, moving it as far as possible from structured, agenda-led therapy. You pick no topic in advance; you lie down, wait, and whatever the body brings forward becomes the session.
modalities.coreIdea: Trusting the body to choose what needs attention, with no agenda and no aim to change it, may surface concerns a planned session would skip.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down somewhere quiet for 20 to 30 minutes with no topic and no technique. Wait until some bodily sense stands out and keep it company without trying to name or change it; if words or images arrive, welcome them, but they are not required.
modalities.whoItsFor: People worn out by worksheets, goals and self-improvement plans who want an open, body-led way to listen to themselves.
modalities.cautions: Without structure, unexpected feelings or memories can surface, so keep the freedom to sit up, open your eyes and stop. Anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should use it only with a qualified therapist, and it is an untested idea rather than a treatment.
modalities.tweet: What if your body set the agenda? Let the Body Choose is a new idea: lie down with no topic, no steps and no goal, and keep company with whatever sense stands out. For people tired of worksheets and self-improvement plans.

modalities.name: How Old Is This
modalities.tagline: Stay inside a feeling and sense how long you have known it.
modalities.whatItIs: How Old Is This is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from action plans and from stepping back to watch your thoughts. Instead of observing a feeling from a distance and turning it into a next step, you let yourself be fully inside its bodily sense and gently notice whether it feels new or long familiar.
modalities.coreIdea: Many bodily feelings carry a sense of age, and simply sensing how familiar a feeling is, without acting on it, may give it room to be understood.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit or lie down for about 20 minutes, let the bodily sense of a current feeling fill your attention, and stay inside it rather than watching it. Then quietly ask "how old does this feel?", receive whatever comes (a year, a place or just "very old"), and finish without making any plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice the same feelings returning and want a calm, self-led way to sense where they come from without analyzing them.
modalities.cautions: Asking about the age of a feeling can bring old memories forward, so go slowly, stop if it gets intense, and work with a trauma-trained therapist if painful memories keep surfacing. It is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Ever had a feeling that seems older than the situation? New concept: How Old Is This. You stay inside a feeling's bodily sense and simply ask how old it feels, with no action plan. A quiet way to sense where your patterns come from.

modalities.name: The No-Why Pause
modalities.tagline: Rest with a tense spot without asking why it is there.
modalities.whatItIs: The No-Why Pause is a proposed practice that takes Focusing far from therapies that search for the hidden emotional reason behind a symptom. You sense a tension, ache or unease in the body and deliberately do not ask why it is there or what it means, letting the sense simply settle.
modalities.coreIdea: Not every bodily feeling needs an explanation, and resting with one without decoding it may be calming in its own right.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 15 minutes and let attention drift to wherever the body feels tense or uneasy. Each time a "why" or a theory arrives, put it down and come back to the plain sense of the place, letting your breathing slow on its own.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of analyzing their reactions and want a calm, self-led way to rest with them instead.
modalities.cautions: Do not use it to ignore new or worrying physical symptoms: get unexplained pain or changes checked by a doctor. Strong feelings can still surface, and this untested idea is not a replacement for therapy when you need it.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: The No-Why Pause. Notice a tense or uneasy spot in your body and skip the usual question of why it's there. No theories, no decoding, just letting the feeling settle. For anyone worn out by analyzing themselves.

modalities.name: Fitting Image Pairs
modalities.tagline: Two friends take turns finding the image that fits a feeling.
modalities.whatItIs: Fitting Image Pairs is a new concept that moves Focusing away from body exercises and toward images and words. Two people take turns: the explorer lets the felt sense of a situation show up as a metaphor (a kind of weather, a place, an object) while the other listens and reflects it back.
modalities.coreIdea: A well-fitting metaphor can hold a vague feeling better than a list of sensations, and checking that it fits may open the situation up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Meet a trusted partner for about 40 minutes and take turns of 15 to 20 minutes each. The explorer asks "if this situation were weather or a place, what would it be?" and checks the image against their inner sense until it fits, while the listener only repeats back the images and adds no advice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body sensations hard to read but think easily in pictures, and who like exploring with a friend.
modalities.cautions: Images can lead into painful memories, so either partner can pause or stop at any time, and listeners should not interpret or push. People with severe trauma, psychosis or dissociation should explore with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: If your week were weather, what would it be? Fitting Image Pairs is a new idea: two friends take turns finding the image that fits a vague feeling, and the listener just reflects it back. For people who think in pictures more than sensations.

modalities.name: Crossroads Body Check
modalities.tagline: A five-minute, do-it-yourself way to include your gut in decisions.
modalities.whatItIs: Crossroads Body Check is a speculative, self-run practice that pushes Focusing away from coach-led depth work and toward everyday use. When you face a choice, you hold each option in mind in turn, notice the bodily sense each one brings, and weigh that alongside your usual reasoning.
modalities.coreIdea: The body often registers a choice before the mind can explain it, and a short, repeatable check can bring that information into ordinary decisions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Write down two or three options, then for each one sit for two or three minutes, imagine having chosen it and notice the felt sense (open, heavy, jittery, light). Jot one word for each, compare the words with your reasons, and decide on one small next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get stuck going back and forth on decisions and want a quick, structured way to include how they feel, without needing a coach.
modalities.cautions: A felt sense is information, not a verdict, so weigh it with facts and advice, especially for money, health or legal decisions. It is a new, untested practice, and a life crisis calls for support from people you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Stuck between two choices? New concept: Crossroads Body Check. Picture having chosen each option, notice how your body responds, jot one word, then weigh it with your reasons. A five-minute, do-it-yourself way to include your gut.

modalities.name: Three-Round Listening Circle
modalities.tagline: Small group, timed turns, three set prompts, one next step.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Round Listening Circle is a new concept that takes Focusing in the opposite direction from open, instruction-free meditation: more structure, more company and more willingness to work on something. A small group meets for timed rounds with set prompts, so everyone gets turns to focus while the others listen.
modalities.coreIdea: A fixed format and a circle of listeners can make inner listening easier to start, keep up and carry toward a next step.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to six people meet for 90 minutes with a facilitator who has learned the format, and each person takes three short rounds: "what am I carrying?", "what is the felt sense of one thing?" and "what small step does it want?". Listeners only reflect back key words, and the session ends with each person naming one step to try.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like structure and company, and who find solo inner work hard to keep up.
modalities.cautions: Groups can feel exposing, so anyone may pass on a round, and what is shared stays in the room. Strong feelings can come up, people in crisis or with severe trauma should get individual professional support, and it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who like structure: the Three-Round Listening Circle. A small group, timed turns, three set prompts and listeners who only reflect back. Everyone leaves with one small next step. Untested, but simple to try.

modalities.name: Room for Mixed Feelings
modalities.tagline: Let love and resentment sit side by side, unresolved.
modalities.whatItIs: Room for Mixed Feelings is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from meditations that build one warm feeling. Instead of growing goodwill, you sense the whole tangle of a situation in the body, such as love and resentment together, and let both be there without resolving them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many situations feel two ways at once, and allowing the mixed bodily sense, instead of forcing one pleasant feeling, may be more honest and less tiring.
modalities.whatYouDo: Bring to mind a person or situation you feel torn about and, for about 20 minutes, notice where each feeling sits in the body. A quiet companion can sit with you and only say back what you name, and you end by acknowledging that both feelings are present, with nothing decided.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel guilty about having mixed feelings toward family, partners or work, and want a gentle way to let them be.
modalities.cautions: Sitting with conflicted feelings about close people can stir grief or anger, so keep sessions short and stop if it becomes overwhelming. If a relationship involves abuse or danger, safety and professional support come first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Love and resentment at the same time? New concept: Room for Mixed Feelings. Instead of trying to feel only kindness, you notice where each feeling sits in your body and let both stay. For anyone torn about someone close.

modalities.name: Life Chapter Listening
modalities.tagline: Feel a whole period of your life at once, then title it.
modalities.whatItIs: Life Chapter Listening is a new concept that pushes Focusing away from precise, structured observation of sensations and toward meaning and story. You take a whole period of your life, such as a year, a job or a move, and let a single felt sense of that chapter form while a friend listens.
modalities.coreIdea: A chapter of life can be felt all at once as a bodily whole, and finding words or images for it may clarify what that time meant.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trusted listener, spend 30 to 40 minutes on one chapter: name it, let its overall felt sense form, then let images, titles or phrases come and check each against that sense. The listener reflects back only your words, and afterwards you write a short title for the chapter.
modalities.whoItsFor: People at a turning point, such as a breakup, a career change or a big birthday, who want to make sense of a period of their life.
modalities.cautions: Looking back over a hard period can stir grief or old pain, so choose a chapter you feel ready for and stop if you feel flooded. People with traumatic histories should do this with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what does a whole year of your life feel like, all at once? Life Chapter Listening has you sense one chapter (a job, a move, a relationship) as a single bodily feeling and find its title, with a friend listening.

modalities.name: One Unhurried Hour
modalities.tagline: One hour, lying still, with a single feeling and no hurry.
modalities.whatItIs: One Unhurried Hour is a proposed practice that takes Focusing as far as possible from fast, intense effort. You spend a full hour lying still with one felt sense, letting long silences pass and never hurrying it.
modalities.coreIdea: Slowing to the gentlest possible pace may let a felt sense unfold in ways a quick check-in never allows.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, lie down somewhere quiet for an hour with a blanket, choose one concern and let its felt sense form. Stay with it with no goal and no timeline, letting minutes pass between words, and afterwards write a few lines about anything that came.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who live at high speed, or whose usual reflection feels rushed, and who want one unhurried hour a week.
modalities.cautions: An hour of stillness can bring old memories or heavy feelings to the surface, so you can stop at any point, and people with trauma or dissociation should do it only with a qualified therapist. If you feel very low or numb, talk to a doctor; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: New idea for people who live at full speed: One Unhurried Hour. Once a week, lie still for an hour with one feeling and let it unfold slowly, with long silences and no goal. The opposite of a workout, on purpose.

modalities.name: Slow Ink Pages
modalities.tagline: Alone with a notebook, writing a feeling slowly, word by word.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Ink Pages is a speculative practice that moves Focusing far from teams, noise and competition, into complete solitude on the page. Alone and seated, you write very slowly from a felt sense, letting images and memories appear in the writing.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing alone, at the speed of the felt sense, can give a vague feeling the time and privacy to find its words.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone with a notebook for 30 minutes, let the felt sense of one situation form, and write only what comes from it, a few words at a time, pausing to check each phrase against the feeling. Nobody reads it, and you can keep it, throw it away or reread it in a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Introverts and people who think better on paper, or who have no listening partner but want to explore what they feel.
modalities.cautions: Writing about the past can bring up painful memories, so stop if you feel flooded and bring lasting distress to a therapist. It is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who think better on paper: Slow Ink Pages. Alone with a notebook, you let a vague feeling form and write only what comes from it, a few words at a time. No audience, no team, no hurry.

modalities.name: Three-Minute Felt Pauses
modalities.tagline: Short guided recordings to notice how you are, several times a day.
modalities.whatItIs: Three-Minute Felt Pauses is a new concept that takes Focusing away from long, steady effort and toward short, guided moments. A teacher records brief guided pauses, and you use them a few times a day, sitting or lying down, to notice a felt sense without any effort.
modalities.coreIdea: Very short guided pauses that ask nothing of your stamina may make inner listening easier to keep up than long sessions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Learn the basics from a Focusing teacher, then use their three-minute recordings two or three times a day: close your eyes, let a felt sense of how you are form, give it a word and let it be. Once a week, a longer guided session lets you stay with something that keeps returning.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with little time or energy, such as busy parents or people living with long-term fatigue, who want inner listening in small doses.
modalities.cautions: Even short pauses can bring up old feelings, and the weekly longer session is best guided by a qualified teacher or therapist if your history includes trauma. It is an untested idea and does not replace medical care for fatigue or low mood.
modalities.tweet: What if inner listening took three minutes, not an hour? Three-Minute Felt Pauses is a new idea: short guided recordings you use a few times a day to notice how you are. No effort or stamina needed. Made for tired, busy people.

modalities.name: Soft Spot Company
modalities.tagline: Keep your tired, tender places company, with nothing to improve.
modalities.whatItIs: Soft Spot Company is a speculative practice that moves Focusing as far as possible from building strength and tracking progress. You turn kindly toward the places where you feel weak, tired or tender and keep them company without trying to make them stronger.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting weakness and tenderness be felt, rather than overcome, may ease the strain of always having to be strong.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 20 minutes and ask where in your body or your life you feel soft, tired or fragile right now. Rest your attention there as you would sit with a tired friend, let images or memories come if they do, and set no goal and keep no record.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always the strong one, or who push through everything, and want a gentle, self-led way to let themselves be tired.
modalities.cautions: Old hurts can surface when you turn toward tender places, so go slowly, stop if it becomes too much and see a therapist if painful feelings persist. Tiredness that does not lift can have medical causes worth checking with a doctor; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Always the strong one? New concept: Soft Spot Company. Lie down, find where you feel tired or tender, and keep that place company, with no goal of getting stronger and nothing to track. An idea for people who push through everything.

modalities.name: The Shy Guest Wait
modalities.tagline: Leave an inner door open and wait warmly for what arrives.
modalities.whatItIs: The Shy Guest Wait is a new concept that takes Focusing away from contact with a real companion and toward a solitary, imagined relationship with your own inner sense. You picture the felt sense as a shy guest who arrives in its own time, and your only job is to wait warmly.
modalities.coreIdea: Treating a hard-to-reach feeling like a shy guest, rather than chasing it, may let it show itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit for 15 to 20 minutes, picture leaving a door open inside you and wait without searching. If something shows up, a sensation, an image or a word, greet it, let it stay as long as it likes and do not question it; if nothing comes, the waiting itself was the practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find that their feelings go quiet the moment they look for them, and who want a self-led practice with no pressure.
modalities.cautions: Waiting in silence can bring unexpected feelings or memories, so keep the right to stop, and get support from a therapist if they are distressing. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for care.
modalities.tweet: Feelings that hide when you look for them? Proposed practice: The Shy Guest Wait. Picture leaving a door open inside you and wait, warmly, for whatever wants to show up. No chasing, no questions. An idea to try on your own.

modalities.name: Kitchen Table Felt Sense
modalities.tagline: Pause mid-conversation to ask how it feels, and actually wait.
modalities.whatItIs: Kitchen Table Felt Sense is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from set forms and formal sessions into ordinary conversation. Friends or family agree that, while talking over tea or a meal, any of them can pause and ask "how does that feel in you?" and wait for the answer.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner listening does not need a ritual; a shared habit of pausing in everyday talk can bring the felt sense into daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Agree on the habit with one or two people you talk with regularly. When someone speaks about something that matters, another asks how it feels in them, both pause for a few breaths while the speaker checks inside, and the conversation carries on, sometimes in a new direction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like the idea of inner listening but will never sit down for a formal session, and households that want warmer conversations.
modalities.cautions: Not every moment suits inner questions, so anyone can decline, and the habit should never be used to pressure or analyze someone. Serious distress needs proper support; this is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Kitchen Table Felt Sense. Over tea or dinner, friends can pause and ask "how does that feel in you?" and actually wait. No formal session, no technique. Just slower, warmer conversations at home.

modalities.name: Private Body Atlas
modalities.tagline: Visit six body regions in order and map how you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Private Body Atlas is a new concept that takes Focusing away from social contact and into a quiet, structured solo routine. Lying alone, you visit regions of the body in a set order and let a small felt sense form in each one, building a private map of how you are.
modalities.coreIdea: Each part of the body can hold its own felt sense of your life, and visiting them in a set order may reveal patterns that a single check misses.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the routine from a teacher, lie down alone for 30 minutes and move through six regions (feet and legs, belly, chest, throat, face, back), asking each "what is the sense here about my life right now?". Write one word per region, and over the weeks look back at how the map changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who need solitude to recharge and like a calm, orderly practice they can do alone.
modalities.cautions: This is not a medical check, so new or persistent pain needs a doctor. Some body areas can hold painful associations, so skip any region that feels unsafe, and people with trauma or dissociation should work with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept for people who recharge alone: Private Body Atlas. Lying down, you visit six body regions in order and ask each what it senses about your life now, then write one word per region. Over weeks, a private map appears.

modalities.name: Felt Shape Sketching
modalities.tagline: Draw a feeling as a shape or color until it fits.
modalities.whatItIs: Felt Shape Sketching is a speculative practice that moves Focusing indoors, onto paper and into a structured, guided format. A teacher guides you to let a felt sense form, draw it as a simple shape or color, look at the drawing and adjust it until it fits.
modalities.coreIdea: Some feelings fit a shape or color before they fit a word, and drawing them step by step gives the felt sense another way to show itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 45-minute session at a table with paper and crayons, a teacher leads you through set steps: sense, draw, look, check, redraw. You need no drawing skill, memories that appear in the picture are noticed but not dug into, and you finish by giving the final drawing a title.
modalities.whoItsFor: Visual people, people whose words come slowly, and anyone who wants a calm indoor activity with a teacher's structure.
modalities.cautions: Images can bring up memories unexpectedly, so the teacher should go at your pace and you can stop at any time; with significant trauma, work with a qualified therapist. It is an untested concept and not a form of art therapy.
modalities.tweet: Some feelings fit a shape before they fit a word. Felt Shape Sketching is a new idea: a teacher guides you to sense a feeling, draw it as a shape or color, and adjust it until it fits. No drawing skill needed.

modalities.name: Between Us Sensing
modalities.tagline: Feel the sense of a relationship and find words for it.
modalities.whatItIs: Between Us Sensing is a new concept that takes Focusing away from raw sensory contact and toward the imagined space between you and another person. With a listener, you bring a relationship to mind, let the felt sense of "how it is between us" form and then find words for it.
modalities.coreIdea: Every relationship has its own felt sense, and naming it carefully may show what you want or fear in that relationship.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained listener, spend 45 minutes on one relationship: picture the person, notice the bodily sense of being with them and find a word or image that fits. If it echoes older relationships, notice that gently, and end by naming one thing you now know about what you want.
modalities.whoItsFor: People puzzling over a friendship, family tie or partnership who want to understand their own side before talking with the other person.
modalities.cautions: Exploring close relationships can stir old attachment pain, so go slowly and stop when you need to, and people with trauma histories should work with a qualified therapist. If a relationship is abusive or unsafe, contact support services; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Confused about where you stand with someone? Between Us Sensing is a proposed practice: picture the person, feel the sense of how it is between you, and find words for it with a listener. A way to understand your own side first.

modalities.name: Quiet After the Noise
modalities.tagline: Fifteen silent minutes to let a loud day settle.
modalities.whatItIs: Quiet After the Noise is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from sound, rhythm and shared expression and into silence. After a loud or busy day, you sit alone in a quiet room and let the felt sense of the day settle, without speaking or playing anything.
modalities.coreIdea: Silence gives the felt sense of a crowded day room to show itself, so it can settle rather than keep ringing on.
modalities.whatYouDo: At the end of a noisy day, switch off sound and screens and sit for 15 minutes in the quietest room you have, with earplugs if needed. Let a felt sense of the whole day form, keep any word for it silent, and let it be there as your breathing slows.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who work in noisy places, care for young children or come home overstimulated, and want a calm, solo way to land.
modalities.cautions: Silence can make worries louder at first; if that happens, shorten the session or allow gentle background sound. It is an untested idea, and lasting anxiety or low mood deserves a talk with a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Home after a loud day and still buzzing? An idea: Quiet After the Noise. Fifteen minutes in a silent room, no music, no screens, just letting the feeling of the whole day settle. A new concept for overstimulated people.

modalities.name: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings
modalities.tagline: Meet a coach eyes open, in the real room, right now.
modalities.whatItIs: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings is a new concept that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from structured imagery work and toward plain contact in the present. Coach and client sit facing each other with eyes open, and the session stays with what is actually here: the room, the light, each other's faces and the feelings that arise between them.
modalities.coreIdea: Being fully seen and present with another person, in real time and without inner images, may itself let held-back feelings soften.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session, you sit across from a trained coach, eyes open, and describe what you notice in the room, in your body and in being looked at kindly. There is no set sequence, and when memories or images pull you away, the coach gently invites you back to what you can see and feel now.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get lost in their heads or in the past and want a slow, warm practice of being present with another person.
modalities.cautions: Being looked at closely can feel exposing or stir old shame, so you can look away, pause or ask for more distance at any time. It is an untested idea offered as coaching, not therapy, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a qualified mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings. You sit with a coach, eyes open, and stay with what is actually here: the room, your body, being kindly seen. No imagery, no script. For people who live in their heads or in the past.

modalities.name: No Parts, Just Awareness
modalities.tagline: No parts to sort: rest as the awareness noticing everything.
modalities.whatItIs: No Parts, Just Awareness is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from parts work and toward a calm, undivided sense of being. Rather than meeting inner parts one by one, the coach invites you to rest as the open awareness in which every feeling, thought and sensation appears.
modalities.coreIdea: When inner conflict is held in a wide, calm awareness instead of being sorted into parts, it may lose some of its grip.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet one-to-one session of about an hour, a coach with meditation training guides you to notice sounds, sensations and feelings, then asks simple questions such as "what is aware of this?" and leaves long pauses. If a strong feeling appears, you let it sit inside that awareness rather than turning it into a part to talk with.
modalities.whoItsFor: People already drawn to meditation who feel worn down by inner arguments and want a calm, guided way to step out of them.
modalities.cautions: Spacious states can feel unsettling or unreal to some people, and deep meditative states can bring up strong feelings, so choose an experienced guide and go at your own pace. People with dissociation, psychosis or severe trauma should work with a qualified clinician; this is an untested coaching idea, not treatment.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people tired of inner arguments: No Parts, Just Awareness. Instead of sorting yourself into parts, a guide helps you rest as the calm awareness that notices every feeling. Untested, gentle, and best with an experienced teacher.

modalities.name: Pure Witness Hours
modalities.tagline: Old feelings met in the body and simply witnessed, not changed.
modalities.whatItIs: Pure Witness Hours is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from structured, change-focused therapy. A trained clinician offers sessions with no agenda, no exercises and no goal of changing anything; old feelings are allowed to arise in the body and are simply witnessed, slowly and kindly.
modalities.coreIdea: Old emotional pain that was never witnessed may need company more than correction, so being witnessed without any push to change becomes the whole method.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you lie or sit comfortably and notice what the body brings up, often feelings that seem to belong to earlier years. The therapist says little beyond reflecting what you notice and checking that you feel steady, and you decide when to slow down or stop.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have done a lot of practical, skills-based therapy and still carry old feelings that want to be felt and witnessed rather than managed.
modalities.cautions: Going deep into old emotional material can be intense, so this should only be done with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, at your own pace, with a plan for staying grounded between sessions. It is an untested concept, not suitable during a crisis, and not a replacement for well-tested treatments for PTSD or depression.
modalities.tweet: What if being witnessed was the whole method? Pure Witness Hours is a new idea: a trauma-trained therapist keeps you company as old feelings rise in the body, with no agenda and no push to change them. Untested and slow on purpose.

modalities.name: Decade by Decade Unfolding
modalities.tagline: Walk slowly through your life story, felt in the body.
modalities.whatItIs: Decade by Decade Unfolding is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from present-moment skills and action plans and toward the whole arc of your life. Over a series of sessions, you revisit each decade of your life and let its felt sense unfold, with no goals and no homework.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling your way through your own history in order, and in the body, may show how old learnings shaped the person you are now.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about ten fortnightly sessions with a licensed therapist or trauma-trained coach, you take one decade at a time, starting with early childhood: name a few places and people, notice what you feel in the body and let words come from that. Nothing is turned into a plan, and you can skip or postpone any period that feels too raw.
modalities.whoItsFor: People at midlife or after a big loss who want to understand their life as a whole, in a slow and contemplative way.
modalities.cautions: Revisiting childhood and painful periods can bring up intense memories, so this needs a practitioner trained in trauma and a pace you control, and people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a licensed mental health professional. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: revisit your whole life, one decade per session, and feel each period in your body instead of analyzing it. Decade by Decade Unfolding pairs you with a trauma-trained guide, with no goals and no homework.

modalities.name: Blanket Rest Sessions
modalities.tagline: Lie down, be accompanied, and let rest be the work.
modalities.whatItIs: Blanket Rest Sessions is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from activating, symptom-focused work and toward deep rest. You lie down under a blanket while a trained coach keeps you quiet company, and nothing is worked on unless it arises on its own.
modalities.coreIdea: For someone exhausted by working on themselves, being safely accompanied while resting may let feelings settle and come forward gently.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a dim, warm room, you lie down for an hour while the coach sits nearby, speaking rarely and only to ask what you notice in the body. If a feeling comes, you can say a word about it and let it pass; if nothing comes, you simply rest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are burnt out or depleted, including those tired of therapy-style digging, who want calm, accompanied rest.
modalities.cautions: Exhaustion can have medical causes and burnout can overlap with depression, so check with a doctor if tiredness or low mood persists. Strong feelings can still surface while resting, and this untested coaching idea is not therapy and not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Burnt out on working on yourself? An idea: Blanket Rest Sessions. You lie down under a blanket while a coach keeps quiet company, and nothing gets worked on unless it arises by itself. A new concept where rest is the work.

modalities.name: Two Voices, One Room
modalities.tagline: Two people speak from feeling while a clinician guides both.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Voices, One Room is a speculative practice that takes Aletheia Coaching away from body exercises and toward words, images and relationship. Two people who share a history, such as partners, siblings or old friends, take turns speaking from their feelings while a licensed therapist guides and protects both.
modalities.coreIdea: Speaking from feeling, rather than about it, in front of someone who matters may help both people understand the old patterns between them.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 90-minute sessions, each person in turn speaks slowly from what they feel about a shared situation, using images and memories as they come, while the other only listens and then says back what they heard. The therapist keeps the pace slow, interrupts blaming and helps each person stay with their own experience.
modalities.whoItsFor: Pairs who keep having the same painful conversation and want a slow, guided way to hear each other's inner experience.
modalities.cautions: Working with shared history can stir old hurts, so it needs a therapist trained in couple or family work and in trauma, and it is not suitable where there is violence, coercion or fear of the other person. It is an untested concept, not a replacement for couples therapy when that is needed.
modalities.tweet: Same painful conversation, again and again? New concept: Two Voices, One Room. Two people take turns speaking from their feelings, not about them, while a therapist keeps it slow and safe. An idea for partners, siblings and old friends.

modalities.name: The Steady Companion
modalities.tagline: A long, reliable relationship with one guide is the method.
modalities.whatItIs: The Steady Companion is a new concept that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from self-help techniques and toward the guiding relationship itself. Instead of learning steps, you meet the same trained practitioner weekly over a long period, and being steadily, warmly accompanied becomes the main ingredient.
modalities.coreIdea: A reliable, attuned relationship over time may give feelings that once had no safe place a chance to come out slowly.
modalities.whatYouDo: You meet one licensed therapist or senior trauma-trained coach weekly for a year or more, and each session starts from how you are and follows what you feel. The practitioner also pays attention to how it feels to be with them, including moments of trust, doubt or longing, and talks about those openly with you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who never had a steady, attentive adult in their life and want depth work built on a long, reliable relationship.
modalities.cautions: Long, close work can stir strong attachment feelings and dependence, so the practitioner needs clinical training, supervision and clear boundaries, and the ending should be planned together. It is an untested concept and not a substitute for treatment of serious mental illness.
modalities.tweet: What if the relationship itself was the method? The Steady Companion is a proposed practice: weekly sessions with the same trained guide for a year or more, starting each time from how you are. For people who never had steady support.

modalities.name: Six-Seat Unfolding Circle
modalities.tagline: A small group, a clear format and guided deep inner work.
modalities.whatItIs: Six-Seat Unfolding Circle is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from open, instruction-free meditation and toward a structured small-group format. Six people meet with a licensed facilitator, and each takes guided turns at slow, feeling-based exploration while the group listens with full attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Being witnessed by a small, steady group, within a clear and safe format, may deepen inner work that feels lonely one to one.
modalities.whatYouDo: The circle meets for three hours every two weeks over six months; each meeting opens with ten minutes of shared silence, then two or three people take a 30-minute guided turn while the others hold quiet attention. Each turn ends with listeners saying one thing they felt while witnessing, without advice or analysis.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want depth work but also want to feel less alone in it, and who like a reliable format.
modalities.cautions: Group depth work can stir strong feelings and shame, so the facilitator should be a licensed clinician trained in trauma and group work, members should be screened beforehand, and anyone can pass. It is an untested idea and not suitable for people in crisis.
modalities.tweet: An idea for doing deep inner work without feeling alone: the Six-Seat Unfolding Circle. Six people, a licensed facilitator, guided turns and a group that listens without advice. New, untested, and built on a clear, safe format.

modalities.name: Unsweetened Feeling Sessions
modalities.tagline: Hard feelings may stay hard, and someone witnesses them.
modalities.whatItIs: Unsweetened Feeling Sessions is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from meditations that build warm, positive feelings. Grief, anger, envy or despair are met in the body and allowed to stay exactly as they are, without being turned into compassion or goodwill, while a trained guide keeps you company.
modalities.coreIdea: Feelings that are always softened or reframed may never be fully felt, and letting them stay unsweetened, with support, may let them run their course.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute one-to-one sessions with a trauma-trained practitioner, you name a hard feeling, find where it lives in the body and let it be as strong as it is, while the guide reflects what they notice. You can bring a trusted friend to sit in silently, and you never have to forgive, reframe or find a lesson.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel pushed to be positive, forgiving or grateful and want a place where hard feelings are allowed.
modalities.cautions: Strong grief or anger can be overwhelming, so sessions need a practitioner trained in trauma, a steady pace and time to settle before leaving. If anger comes with urges to harm anyone, or despair with thoughts of suicide, get professional help straight away; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Tired of being told to look on the bright side? Unsweetened Feeling Sessions is a new concept: grief or anger is felt in the body and allowed to stay as it is, with a trained guide beside you. No forced forgiveness, no lessons.

modalities.name: Dreams Felt Slowly
modalities.tagline: Bring a dream and let its felt meaning unfold slowly.
modalities.whatItIs: Dreams Felt Slowly is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from careful observation of the senses and toward the imagery of dreams. You bring a recent dream, and a guide helps you feel your way into its images, mood and bodily sense, letting meaning unfold without a fixed method of interpretation.
modalities.coreIdea: Dreams carry feelings in picture form, and slowly sensing them, rather than decoding them with a dictionary of symbols, may bring old emotional themes into awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: You write down a dream on waking and bring it to a 60-minute session with a trained coach, one to one or in a small dream group of four. You retell it in the present tense, pause on the image that feels most charged, notice the body's response and let words come, while the guide asks only open questions.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with vivid dreams who are curious about what those dreams might hold and like an imaginative, unhurried style.
modalities.cautions: Dreams can carry distressing material, and recurring nightmares or trauma-related dreams call for a licensed therapist rather than coaching. This is an untested concept and offers no fixed answers about what dreams mean.
modalities.tweet: Curious what your dreams carry? Dreams Felt Slowly is a proposed practice: retell a dream in the present tense, pause on its most charged image, and let its feeling unfold with a guide. No symbol dictionary, just slow attention.

modalities.name: At Half Speed
modalities.tagline: Deep inner work done at half the pace of ordinary talk.
modalities.whatItIs: At Half Speed is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from fast, intense effort. Everything in the session happens at half the usual pace, with long pauses after every sentence, so that deep and old feelings are only ever approached slowly and in stillness.
modalities.coreIdea: Radical slowness may be what makes deep material bearable: at half speed there is always time to notice, settle and choose whether to go on.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma, you sit or lie very still, and both of you speak in short phrases separated by long pauses. Whenever something old or painful stirs, the therapist slows things down further and checks that you feel steady before you stay with it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who talk fast, rush past their feelings or feel flooded when deep material comes too quickly.
modalities.cautions: Slowness lowers but does not remove the intensity of deep work, so it needs a licensed clinician experienced in trauma and a pace you can stop at any time. It is an untested idea, not suitable during a crisis, and not a replacement for well-tested trauma treatment.
modalities.tweet: New concept: At Half Speed. Deep inner work where everything happens at half the usual pace, with long pauses after every sentence and a trauma-trained therapist beside you. An idea for people who rush past their own feelings.

modalities.name: Guided Cabin Solitude
modalities.tagline: Days alone in a quiet place, with one guided talk a day.
modalities.whatItIs: Guided Cabin Solitude is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from teams, games and constant company into deep solitude. You spend a few days alone in a quiet place, letting inner images and old feelings come in their own time, and meet a trained guide once a day to make sense of what arose.
modalities.coreIdea: Long stretches of solitude can let deep feelings surface that never appear in a busy week, and a daily meeting with a guide keeps that safe and digestible.
modalities.whatYouDo: For three to five days you stay alone in a simple cabin or retreat room with no phone, spending the days resting, sitting, writing and noticing images, memories and moods. Each day you have a one-hour session with a licensed therapist or trauma-trained coach, who is also reachable at any hour if you need support.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced inner explorers, not in crisis, who want an extended, solitary stretch of depth work with a safety net.
modalities.cautions: Solitude and intensive inner work can bring up difficult experiences, including fear, panic or unreal feelings, so participants should be screened first, and people with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should not do this without their clinician's agreement. It is an untested idea, and you can end the stay early at any time.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: three days alone in a quiet cabin, no phone, letting old feelings surface in their own time, with one talk a day with a trained guide. Guided Cabin Solitude, an untested idea for experienced inner explorers.

modalities.name: The Long Interval
modalities.tagline: One deep session, then weeks for life to do its part.
modalities.whatItIs: The Long Interval is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from steady, sustained effort and toward deliberate gaps. Deep sessions with a trained guide are spaced a month or more apart, with no homework in between, because the time between sessions is treated as part of the work.
modalities.coreIdea: What shifts in a deep session may need weeks of ordinary life to settle, so spacing sessions widely puts rest, not persistence, at the center.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every four to six weeks you have a 90-minute session with a licensed therapist or trauma-trained coach, where you slowly feel into what has been stirring and let it be met. Between sessions you do nothing special, apart from a short check-in message two weeks later and the option to call if something difficult comes up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cannot manage weekly sessions, feel overloaded by homework, or prefer to let things settle in their own time.
modalities.cautions: Deep material opened in one session can stir things up in the weeks that follow, so the practitioner should be licensed, trained in trauma and reachable between sessions. It is an untested idea and not suitable for anyone in crisis or needing regular treatment.
modalities.tweet: What if the weeks between sessions were part of the work? An idea: The Long Interval. One deep session with a trained guide every month or so, no homework, and time for life to let things settle. A new concept for people who feel overloaded.

modalities.name: Nothing Measured Here
modalities.tagline: Deep work with no goals, scores or progress reports.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing Measured Here is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from progressive overload and tracked progress. Sessions have no goals, rating scales or talk of improvement; you simply explore what you feel, often reaching old feelings, and nobody measures how far you have come.
modalities.coreIdea: When nothing is measured, there is no way to fail, and that may let people stop performing their own growth and meet what they actually feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly one-hour sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma, you begin wherever you are and follow your feelings, thoughts and memories, mostly in words. The therapist never asks for scores or progress updates but still watches carefully for your safety and wellbeing.
modalities.whoItsFor: Perfectionists and high achievers who turn even therapy into a project and want a place with nothing to achieve.
modalities.cautions: Not measuring progress does not mean ignoring risk: if your mood worsens or you feel unsafe, say so and seek extra help, and the therapist should check this regularly. It is an untested idea, best with a licensed clinician, and not a replacement for treatment of depression or other conditions.
modalities.tweet: Do you turn even self-care into a project? New concept: Nothing Measured Here. Deep sessions with a therapist where nothing is scored, tracked or improved; you just meet what you feel. An idea for perfectionists.

modalities.name: Childhood Rooms Revisited
modalities.tagline: A guided imagined walk through the rooms you grew up in.
modalities.whatItIs: Childhood Rooms Revisited is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from outward contact with real companions and toward inner imagery of the past. With a trained guide, you imagine walking through the rooms of a home you grew up in and notice the felt sense each room brings.
modalities.coreIdea: Places hold feelings, and slowly revisiting remembered rooms in imagination may bring old emotional learnings gently into awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions, a trauma-trained therapist invites you to picture the front door of a childhood home and move at your own pace from room to room, describing what you see and feel in the body. You choose which doors to open and can step back outside at any moment, and the guide never suggests what you should find.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about how their early home shaped their feelings today, who think easily in pictures.
modalities.cautions: Imagery of childhood can bring up painful memories, and imagined scenes are not a reliable record of what happened, so this needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma who avoids leading questions. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should only do it as part of their own treatment; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Places hold feelings. Childhood Rooms Revisited is a proposed practice: with a trauma-trained guide, you imagine walking through the home you grew up in, room by room, choosing which doors to open. A new idea, done slowly.

modalities.name: Say It Unedited
modalities.tagline: Speak whatever comes, unedited, while a guide tracks the feeling.
modalities.whatItIs: Say It Unedited is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from set forms and body routines and toward free, unstructured speech. You say whatever comes to mind without tidying it, and a trained guide listens for the feeling under the words and slows you down when something important stirs.
modalities.coreIdea: Unedited speech lets feelings slip past the inner editor, and pausing on the moments that carry feeling may open the way to older emotional material.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly one-hour sessions with a licensed therapist, you sit back and talk freely, including half-thoughts, odd images and things that seem irrelevant. When your voice changes or your body reacts, the therapist asks you to pause and feel what is there, then lets the talk flow on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rehearse everything they say and want a place where nothing needs to make sense.
modalities.cautions: Free speech can lead quickly into painful memories or shame, so the therapist should be licensed and trained in trauma, and you can pause or change the subject at any time. It is an untested idea and not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Ever rehearse everything you say? Say It Unedited is a new idea: talk freely, half-thoughts and all, while a therapist listens for the feeling under the words and slows you down when something stirs. Untested, and nothing has to make sense.

modalities.name: The Untold Story Room
modalities.tagline: Do deep work without ever telling what happened.
modalities.whatItIs: The Untold Story Room is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from sharing and social connection and toward complete privacy. You never have to say what happened: you bring a memory to mind privately and report only what you notice in your body, while a trained guide helps you stay calm and steady.
modalities.coreIdea: Some experiences are too private or painful to put into words, and working only with the body's response may let them be met without being told.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma, you lie or sit comfortably, silently recall something that still troubles you, and say only words like "tight chest" or "warmth in my hands". The therapist guides you to notice those sensations, pause and settle, following a simple, repeatable routine.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry experiences they cannot or will not describe, or who feel exposed by talking.
modalities.cautions: Recalling painful memories, even silently, can be intense, so this belongs only with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, who will check how steady you feel throughout. It is an untested idea and not a replacement for well-tested trauma treatment.
modalities.tweet: Some things are too private to say out loud. The Untold Story Room is a new concept: you recall a memory silently and report only what you feel in your body, while a trauma-trained therapist keeps you steady. Your story stays yours.

modalities.name: Letters Never Sent
modalities.tagline: Write to people from your past, read aloud, feel the response.
modalities.whatItIs: Letters Never Sent is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching indoors, onto the page and deep into personal history. You write letters you will never send to people from your past, read them aloud to a trained guide and stay with what you feel as you hear your own words.
modalities.coreIdea: Saying what was never said, in a letter no one will receive, may bring old feelings into the open where they can be felt and met.
modalities.whatYouDo: Between sessions you write one letter by hand to someone who mattered, such as a parent, a former partner or your younger self. In the next 75-minute session you read it aloud slowly to a licensed therapist, pausing whenever a line stirs something, and the therapist helps you notice the feeling in your body.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry words they never got to say and find writing easier than speaking.
modalities.cautions: Letters to people who hurt you can bring up intense pain, so this needs a licensed therapist trained in trauma, and the letters should stay private and unsent. It is an untested idea, not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Words you never got to say? An idea: Letters Never Sent. Write to someone from your past, a letter no one will receive, then read it aloud to a trained guide and stay with what you feel. Untested, private and slow.

modalities.name: Stories We Inherited
modalities.tagline: Explore the family stories you grew up inside.
modalities.whatItIs: Stories We Inherited is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from sensory, present-moment work and toward the family stories that shaped you. With a trained guide, you explore the tales, sayings and unspoken rules passed down in your family and notice how each one still feels in you.
modalities.coreIdea: Family stories carry emotional lessons across generations, and feeling into them may show which ones you still live by.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist, you recall stories and sayings you heard growing up, such as "we don't make a fuss" or the tale of a grandparent's hardship, and let images and feelings come. Later, you can invite a parent, sibling or other relative to one session to share their version, if both of you want to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about how family history, migration or hardship still echoes in their own reactions.
modalities.cautions: Family stories can touch painful or traumatic history, and joint sessions with relatives can stir conflict, so this needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma and family work, and relatives should never be pressured to attend. It is an untested idea, not a replacement for therapy.
modalities.tweet: "We don't make a fuss." Which family sayings still run your life? Stories We Inherited is a proposed practice: explore the stories you grew up inside, with a trained guide, and notice how each one still feels. A new idea.

modalities.name: Mostly Silent Hours
modalities.tagline: Deep sessions held largely in silence, words only when needed.
modalities.whatItIs: Mostly Silent Hours is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from sound, rhythm and expression and toward silence. Sessions are held largely without words: you and a trained guide sit together quietly, and speech happens only when something needs to be said.
modalities.coreIdea: Shared silence can feel safe enough for deep feelings to rise without being explained, and words that come after a long quiet may be the ones that matter.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room, you sit with a licensed therapist or trauma-trained coach for an hour, eyes open or closed, letting feelings and memories come and go. Every so often the guide asks, very softly, what you notice, and you can answer with one word or not at all.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel drained by talking about feelings, or who sense that talking keeps them on the surface.
modalities.cautions: Silence can feel uncomfortable or let distressing memories rise, so agree beforehand on a simple signal for needing to talk or stop, and work with a clinician trained in trauma. It is an untested idea and not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Talked out? Mostly Silent Hours is a new concept: deep sessions with a trained guide held largely in silence, with words only when something needs saying. An untested idea for people who feel that talking keeps them on the surface.

modalities.name: Window Seat Idling
modalities.tagline: Sit at a window, eyes open, and let looking happen.
modalities.whatItIs: Window Seat Idling is a new concept that pushes Do Nothing meditation further from imagery-based therapy, toward the plain outside world. You sit at a window with your eyes open and let looking happen by itself, with no instruction from anyone, no inner pictures to build and no history to explore.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the eyes wander over the real world, without steering them or building inner images, may be one of the simplest ways to rest the mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a window, sit down for 10 to 20 minutes and let your gaze go wherever it goes: clouds, a wall, passing cars, a fly. If you notice yourself trying to look properly or to meditate well, let that go too, and get up whenever you like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find eyes-closed meditation strange or heavy and want a no-instruction rest they can start on their own today.
modalities.cautions: Open sitting can still let worries or difficult feelings surface; if that keeps happening, try a more guided practice or talk to someone you trust. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for anxiety or depression.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Window Seat Idling. Sit at a window, eyes open, and let your gaze wander over clouds, walls and passing cars. No instructions, no visualizing, nothing to get right. A rest you can start today if eyes-closed meditation feels strange.

modalities.name: Let the Voices Talk
modalities.tagline: Inner commentary keeps talking; you simply stop answering it.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Voices Talk is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from therapies that hold conversations with inner parts. When your inner commentary worries, judges or argues, you neither answer it, nor argue back, nor try to quiet it; you let it talk like a radio in another room.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner chatter may lose some of its pull when nobody inside answers it, so not replying becomes a way to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie down for 15 minutes with your eyes open or closed and let sounds, sensations and the running commentary in your head all happen. Each time you catch yourself replying to a thought, reassuring it or arguing with it, drop the reply and let the commentary carry on unanswered.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with busy, chattering minds who are tired of arguing with their own thoughts.
modalities.cautions: If voices seem to come from outside you, or become frightening or commanding, stop and speak with a doctor or mental health professional. It is an untested idea, and people with psychosis, severe trauma or dissociation should not use it in place of professional care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for chattering minds: Let the Voices Talk. When your inner commentary worries or argues, you don't answer it, argue back or shush it. You let it talk like a radio in the next room. For anyone tired of arguing with themselves.

modalities.name: No Clock Sitting
modalities.tagline: Rest with no timer, no streak and no log.
modalities.whatItIs: No Clock Sitting is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation even further from structured, measured therapy. There is no timer, no session length, no log and no technique: you stop, rest and do nothing until you feel like getting up.
modalities.coreIdea: Removing even the clock and the record may take the last trace of performance out of resting.
modalities.whatYouDo: Whenever you have some unclaimed time, sit or lie down without setting a timer or checking the time, and let whatever happens happen. Get up when it feels natural, after two minutes or forty, and do not write it down, count it or rate it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who track everything, from steps to sleep to meditation streaks, and want one thing in life that is never measured.
modalities.cautions: Without limits, long open sits can drift into worry or low mood for some people, so if that happens, stand up and do something active. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for treatment for depression or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: No Clock Sitting. Rest and do nothing with no timer, no session length, no streak and no log, then get up whenever it feels natural. For people who track their steps, sleep and meditation minutes and want one thing never measured.

modalities.name: For No Reason At All
modalities.tagline: Do nothing without doing it for anything.
modalities.whatItIs: For No Reason At All is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from therapies built on values, goals and committed action. You sit and do nothing without doing it for anything: not for calm, not for health, not even to become a better meditator.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing nothing purely for its own sake, without any hoped-for benefit, may free it from the pressure that creeps into wellbeing routines.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit somewhere comfortable for about 15 minutes and, before you start, quietly let go of any reason for sitting. Whenever a hope appears (to relax, to sleep better, to feel less anxious), notice it, drop it too and carry on doing nothing.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have turned rest into another self-improvement task and want rest with no purpose attached.
modalities.cautions: Purposeless sitting can let low mood or worry fill the space, so stop if it feels worse rather than restful. It is an untested idea, and anyone with severe depression or trauma should practice with a qualified teacher and stay in touch with a clinician.
modalities.tweet: What if you rested for no reason at all? Not for calm, not for health, not to improve. For No Reason At All is a new concept: you sit, drop every hoped-for benefit as it appears, and simply do nothing. For people who turned rest into homework.

modalities.name: Self-Work Holiday
modalities.tagline: One protected hour a week off from analyzing yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Self-Work Holiday is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation far from therapies that uncover hidden emotional meanings. Once a week, for an hour, you take a complete holiday from analyzing, decoding or improving yourself and simply rest in the present.
modalities.coreIdea: Constant self-analysis can become its own strain, and a regular, protected break from it may let the mind settle.
modalities.whatYouDo: Pick a weekly hour, put away journals, therapy homework and self-help books, and sit, lie down or look out of the window. If you catch yourself interpreting a feeling or tracing it back to childhood, smile at the habit and come back to the sounds and sensations of the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in therapy or on a personal growth path who feel they never stop working on themselves.
modalities.cautions: A break from self-analysis is not a reason to stop needed treatment, so keep your therapy and medication as agreed with your clinician. It is an untested idea, and if difficult feelings press in during the hour, it is fine to reach out for support.
modalities.tweet: Always working on yourself? An idea: the Self-Work Holiday. One protected hour a week with no journaling, no decoding feelings and no self-improvement, just resting in the room you're in. For people who never take a break from their own growth.

modalities.name: Worry Left Unsolved
modalities.tagline: Let one worry sit there, untouched, for ten minutes.
modalities.whatItIs: Worry Left Unsolved is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from body-based release methods and toward the mind. A worry is allowed to sit in your thoughts while you neither solve it, nor soothe it, nor try to release it through the body; you simply let it be there.
modalities.coreIdea: Many worries grow when we keep trying to settle them, and leaving one unsolved for a few minutes may show that it can be tolerated.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 10 minutes, bring to mind a current worry and then stop doing anything about it: no planning, no reassuring, no breathing techniques. When the mind starts problem-solving, let the attempt drop and let the worry sit there like an unopened letter.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who solve, plan or reassure themselves endlessly and want to practice letting a worry be.
modalities.cautions: If worry is constant, overwhelming or stops you sleeping or functioning, it may be an anxiety problem that deserves professional help. It is an untested idea, and real problems still need practical action at another time.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: let one worry sit there, unsolved, for ten minutes. No planning, no reassuring, no breathing tricks. Worry Left Unsolved is a new idea for people who can't stop problem-solving in their heads.

modalities.name: Wide Attention, No Center
modalities.tagline: Let attention spread over everything, with nothing in the middle.
modalities.whatItIs: Wide Attention, No Center is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation away from practices that gather attention around one inner sense. Instead of focusing in on anything, you let attention spread as wide as it likes, over sounds, the room, thoughts and body, with nothing at the center.
modalities.coreIdea: When attention has no center, no single feeling or thought gets to dominate, which may make the whole field of experience feel lighter.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 15 minutes with your eyes open and soft and let everything you can see, hear, think and feel be included at once. When attention narrows onto one thing, let it widen again, without pushing that thing away.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to zoom in and get stuck on one feeling or problem, and who want a light, self-led way to widen out.
modalities.cautions: Wide, open attention can feel spacey or unreal to some people; if it does, look at one solid object and stop. It is an untested idea, and people with dissociation or psychosis should talk to a clinician before trying open practices.
modalities.tweet: Do you zoom in and get stuck on one worry? Proposed practice: Wide Attention, No Center. Let attention spread over sounds, the room, thoughts and body all at once, with nothing in the middle. A light, new idea you can try alone.

modalities.name: Ten-Second Nothing
modalities.tagline: Stop for ten seconds at everyday cues, many times a day.
modalities.whatItIs: Ten-Second Nothing is a speculative practice that takes Do Nothing meditation away from long guided sessions and deep work and shrinks it to a self-taught pause of about ten seconds. Many times a day, you stop, let whatever is happening happen, then carry on.
modalities.coreIdea: Tiny, frequent moments of not controlling anything may fit into a busy life where a full session never will.
modalities.whatYouDo: Pick everyday cues, such as opening a door, waiting for a kettle or sitting down at your desk, and at each one stop for roughly ten seconds and drop any effort to steer your attention. There is nothing to learn, no app and no teacher, and you go straight back to what you were doing.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who never find 20 minutes to meditate, and beginners who find long sits daunting.
modalities.cautions: Short pauses are low risk, but they are not a treatment for mental health problems, so get support if stress or low mood persists. Do not pause like this while driving or doing anything that needs your full attention; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Can't find 20 minutes to meditate? Try ten seconds. Ten-Second Nothing is an untested idea: at everyday cues like a boiling kettle or a door handle, stop and let whatever is happening happen, then carry on. No app, no teacher.

modalities.name: Welcome the Boredom
modalities.tagline: Let dull, ordinary time stay dull, and stay with it.
modalities.whatItIs: Welcome the Boredom is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from practices that build up warm, pleasant feelings. Instead of cultivating goodwill or bliss, you welcome the flat, dull, boring moments that most meditation tries to get past.
modalities.coreIdea: Boredom is usually escaped within seconds, and letting it be, without making it pleasant, may make ordinary life easier to sit with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit somewhere unremarkable for 15 minutes with no phone, music or book, and let the time feel as dull as it does. When you notice an urge to make it nicer (a pleasant thought, a plan, a fidget), let the urge be and stay with the plain, flat feel of the moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who reach for their phone at every quiet moment and want to get comfortable with ordinary, unexciting time.
modalities.cautions: Feeling flat for a few minutes is normal, but a lasting loss of interest or pleasure can be a sign of depression that deserves a talk with a doctor. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Reach for your phone in every quiet moment? Welcome the Boredom is a new idea: fifteen minutes somewhere unremarkable, no phone or music, letting the time feel as dull as it is. No bliss to chase, just ordinary time. 📵

modalities.name: Fog Allowed Sitting
modalities.tagline: When the mind is hazy, let it stay hazy.
modalities.whatItIs: Fog Allowed Sitting is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from insight practices that observe experience precisely. You make no attempt to see clearly: when the mind is foggy, vague or half-dreaming, you let it stay that way.
modalities.coreIdea: Demanding clarity of a tired mind can become its own strain, so allowing the fog may let rest happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or recline for 15 to 20 minutes, close your eyes or let them unfocus, and let thoughts be blurry and half-formed. You do not label, note or examine anything, and if you notice an effort to see more clearly, you drop it and let the haze be.
modalities.whoItsFor: Tired people, and meditators who feel they must always be alert and precise, who want a gentler, hazier rest.
modalities.cautions: Fogginess that lasts, or new trouble thinking clearly, can have medical causes and should be checked by a doctor. This untested idea is not for moments that need alertness, and people with dissociation should talk to a clinician before trying it.
modalities.tweet: Mind too foggy to meditate? Fog Allowed Sitting is a proposed practice that says fine, stay foggy. No noting, no examining, no effort to see clearly, just letting a hazy mind rest. A new concept for tired brains.

modalities.name: Dozing Permitted Rest
modalities.tagline: The lowest gear possible: rest where drifting off is fine.
modalities.whatItIs: Dozing Permitted Rest is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from intense, timed effort. You lie down and do nothing in the gentlest possible way, and unlike most meditation, drifting into a doze is not a mistake but simply one more thing that can happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Dropping even the expectation of staying awake removes the last effort from rest, which may make it easier for an exhausted mind to let go.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the afternoon or early evening, lie down somewhere comfortable for 20 minutes, close your eyes and let thoughts, sounds and drowsiness come and go. If you fall asleep, fine; if you stay awake, also fine; set a soft alarm so you do not oversleep into the night.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are worn out, and anyone who feels they fail at meditation because they keep nodding off.
modalities.cautions: Constant daytime sleepiness can be a sign of a sleep disorder, low mood or another medical issue worth checking with a doctor, and long late naps can disturb night sleep. Never do this when you need to stay alert, such as before driving; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Keep nodding off when you meditate? New concept: Dozing Permitted Rest. Lie down, let thoughts and drowsiness come and go, and if you drift off, that's fine too. Rest in the lowest gear possible, the opposite of a high-intensity workout.

modalities.name: The Unreachable Half Hour
modalities.tagline: Thirty minutes when nobody can need anything from you.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unreachable Half Hour is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from teams, roles and constant coordination with others. For thirty minutes you make yourself completely unreachable, with phone off and door closed, and do nothing at all.
modalities.coreIdea: Knowing that nobody can call on you, even briefly, may let the part of the mind that is always on standby switch off.
modalities.whatYouDo: Tell anyone who depends on you that you will be unavailable for half an hour, switch your phone off (not just to silent) and close the door. Sit or lie however you like and let whatever happens happen, until the half hour is over.
modalities.whoItsFor: Parents, carers, managers and anyone who is always on call and rarely has time that belongs to nobody else.
modalities.cautions: Only do this when someone else is covering anyone who needs supervision, such as young children or a person you care for. Solitude can let low mood surface, so if it regularly leaves you feeling worse, talk to someone; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: For parents, carers and anyone on call, an idea: The Unreachable Half Hour. Phone off (not on silent), door closed, someone else covering, and thirty minutes when nobody can need anything from you. Untested, but easy to try.

modalities.name: Nowhere to Get To
modalities.tagline: Turn queues, platforms and waiting rooms into rest.
modalities.whatItIs: Nowhere to Get To is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from steady effort toward a distant goal.
