It uses the moments when you are stuck waiting, in queues, on platforms or in waiting rooms, as a chance to stop trying to get anywhere and let whatever happens happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Waiting is usually spent straining toward what comes next, and dropping that strain may turn dead time into rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Learn the idea from a short guide or book, then each time you have to wait, leave your phone in your pocket and stop willing the wait to end. Let your eyes, thoughts and impatience do whatever they do, and when the bus, the queue or the appointment arrives, simply carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Impatient people, commuters and anyone who loses a lot of time to waiting and finds it irritating.
modalities.cautions: Stay aware of your surroundings, your belongings and any traffic, and never do this while driving or cycling. It is an untested idea, and impatience that comes with intense anger or anxiety may deserve professional support.
modalities.tweet: Stuck in a queue again? New idea: Nowhere to Get To. Each time you have to wait, phone stays in your pocket and you stop willing the wait to end. Let thoughts and impatience do what they do. Dead time, turned into rest.

modalities.name: Beside the Undone List
modalities.tagline: Sit next to your to-do list and do nothing about it.
modalities.whatItIs: Beside the Undone List is a speculative practice that takes Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from effort, progress and achievement. You sit near your unfinished tasks, with the to-do list in plain view, and for a set while you do nothing about any of them.
modalities.coreIdea: Resting while tasks remain undone, rather than only after they are finished, may loosen the belief that rest has to be earned.
modalities.whatYouDo: Put your to-do list on the table, sit beside it for 15 minutes and let thoughts about deadlines, guilt and plans come and go without acting on them. When the urge to tick something off appears, let it be an urge, and when the time is up, go back to work normally.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they can only rest once everything is done, which is never.
modalities.cautions: This is not a way to ignore urgent deadlines, bills or safety tasks, so deal with those first. If overwhelm or procrastination is seriously affecting your life, it may help to talk to a doctor or therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Think you have to earn your rest? Beside the Undone List is a new concept: sit next to your to-do list for 15 minutes and do nothing about any of it. Let the guilt and urges come and go. An idea for people who are never done.

modalities.name: Held by the Floor
modalities.tagline: Lie down and let the ground do all the holding.
modalities.whatItIs: Held by the Floor is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from comfort given by a living companion and toward the plain support of the ground. Alone, you lie on the floor and let it hold your whole weight, with no one to look after and nothing to do.
modalities.coreIdea: Feeling fully supported by something that asks nothing back may make it easier to stop holding yourself up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie on a rug or mat, on your back or side, eyes open or closed, for 15 minutes, and let the floor take your weight. Thoughts, images and sounds can come and go; whenever you notice yourself trying to relax properly, let that go and let the floor do the work.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always holding things together for others and want a simple, solitary way to be held for a change.
modalities.cautions: Get down and up slowly, use a mat and cushions if your back or joints complain, and choose a sitting position if lying down is hard. Lying on your back can feel vulnerable for some people, especially after trauma, so lie on your side or sit up if it feels unsafe; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: When did something last hold you up? An idea: Held by the Floor. Lie on a rug for 15 minutes and let the ground take your whole weight, with nothing to do and nobody to look after. A new concept for people who rarely feel held.

modalities.name: Slumped and Unposed
modalities.tagline: No posture, no breathing technique: rest exactly as you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Slumped and Unposed is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from careful postures and regulated breathing. You sit or sprawl in whatever position you happen to be in, slumped on the sofa if that is where you are, and leave the breath and body alone entirely.
modalities.coreIdea: Arranging the body and breath can quietly turn rest into a performance, so leaving them unarranged may remove one more layer of control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Wherever you are sitting or lying, stop for 10 to 20 minutes without straightening up, closing your eyes or adjusting your breath. Let attention drift through thoughts and daydreams, and when you catch yourself fixing your posture or breathing deeply on purpose, let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they cannot meditate because they cannot sit still or upright, and anyone put off by strict postures.
modalities.cautions: Shift position if something starts to ache or go numb, since leaving the body alone does not mean staying in pain. It is an untested idea, and anyone with breathing problems or chronic pain should follow their own clinician's advice.
modalities.tweet: Good news for sofa sprawlers. Slumped and Unposed is a new idea: stay exactly as you are, leave your breath and posture alone, and let your mind drift. No performance, no technique.

modalities.name: Talk-Free Evening
modalities.tagline: An evening of not speaking after a socially full week.
modalities.whatItIs: Talk-Free Evening is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from talk and social contact. After days full of people, you spend an evening alone without speaking, messaging or listening to talk, and simply let the quiet be.
modalities.coreIdea: Speech keeps the social mind running, and a stretch of not talking at all may let it wind down more fully than ordinary rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once you have learned the idea from a short guide, pick an evening, tell the people you live with, and put away your phone and anything with voices in it. Move slowly through ordinary things like making tea or lying on the bed, and in between, sit and do nothing until bedtime.
modalities.whoItsFor: Introverts, people in people-heavy jobs and anyone who feels talked out by the end of the week.
modalities.cautions: Make sure someone can still reach you in an emergency, and do not use silence to avoid people you need to talk to. If you avoid company because of fear or low mood, or the quiet makes you feel worse, talk to a doctor or therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: A week full of people? New concept: the Talk-Free Evening. No speaking, no messaging, no podcasts, just moving slowly through tea and quiet and doing nothing until bed. An untested idea for introverts and people in people-heavy jobs.

modalities.name: Indoor Memory Drift
modalities.tagline: Indoors, eyes closed, letting old memories float by.
modalities.whatItIs: Indoor Memory Drift is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from walking outdoors among sights and sounds. Indoors and still, with your eyes closed, you allow memories that arise to drift through without either pursuing or pushing them away.
modalities.coreIdea: Memories often surface when the mind is idle, and letting them pass like clouds, without reliving or analyzing them, may make them feel less sticky.
modalities.whatYouDo: Learn the idea from a short guide or book, then sit in a comfortable chair for 15 minutes with your eyes closed and let the mind wander. If an old scene or face appears, let it come and go like a passing car, without digging into it or replaying it, and open your eyes whenever you wish.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice memories popping up whenever they stop and want a calm, self-led way to let them pass.
modalities.cautions: Idle time can bring up painful or traumatic memories; if that happens, open your eyes, look around the room, and consider working with a trauma-trained therapist. It is an untested idea and not a way to process trauma alone.
modalities.tweet: Ever notice old memories pop up the moment you stop? An idea: Indoor Memory Drift. Sit with your eyes closed and let memories float by like passing cars, without chasing or pushing them away. A new concept to try gently, alone.

modalities.name: Daydreams Welcome Here
modalities.tagline: No sensory anchor: let the mind wander into daydreams.
modalities.whatItIs: Daydreams Welcome Here is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation away from practices that anchor attention in the senses. Instead of returning to the breath or sounds, you let the mind wander into daydreams, fantasies and plans and stay there as long as it likes.
modalities.coreIdea: Unhurried daydreaming may be a form of rest in its own right, and treating it as welcome rather than as a lapse could take pressure off people who struggle to focus.
modalities.whatYouDo: After reading a short guide, sit or recline for 15 to 20 minutes, close your eyes or look at nothing in particular, and let daydreams unfold. You do not bring attention back to anything; you only drop any effort to steer the daydream, and you stop when you are ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: Natural daydreamers and people who find anchor-based meditation frustrating because their mind keeps wandering.
modalities.cautions: If daydreams turn into worry, replaying arguments or brooding, open your eyes and do something active, since rumination can deepen low mood. Daydreaming that takes over many hours a day deserves a talk with a professional; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Told to keep bringing your wandering mind back? Daydreams Welcome Here is a proposed practice: drop the anchor, close your eyes, and let daydreams unfold for 15 minutes without steering them. A new idea for natural daydreamers.

modalities.name: Earplug Silence Sitting
modalities.tagline: Earplugs in, no input at all, nothing to do.
modalities.whatItIs: Earplug Silence Sitting is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from music, rhythm and shared sound. With earplugs in and no audio of any kind, you sit in as much silence as you can get and let whatever happens happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Removing sound, the one input most of us never switch off, may let the mind settle into a deeper kind of quiet.
modalities.whatYouDo: Put in soft earplugs, sit somewhere comfortable for 15 minutes with your eyes open or closed, and make no effort to listen to anything, including the silence itself. If inner songs or ringing in the ears appear, let them be part of what is happening.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who always have music, podcasts or TV on in the background and wonder what plain quiet feels like.
modalities.cautions: Silence can make ringing in the ears or worries seem louder, so stop if it feels unpleasant, and do not block your hearing when you need to hear children, alarms or traffic. It is an untested idea; keep earplugs clean and do not push them deep into the ear.
modalities.tweet: Music, podcasts, TV, always on? New concept: Earplug Silence Sitting. Fifteen minutes with earplugs in and no input at all, letting whatever happens happen. An untested idea for anyone who never hears plain quiet.
